chapters.title: A map of a running program

scenes.say: Where does each variable in your program actually live? By the end, you'll draw a running program's memory map, and explain what new does that malloc never will.
Today you will do three things. Place every variable in a running program's memory. Follow new down to the allocator. And see what new does that malloc never will.
lines: Follow new down to the allocator
See what new does that malloc never will

scenes.title: Where does each variable live?
scenes.statement: A small program has a global, a static, a local, and a Point made with new. Place each one in memory.

example.input: int g = 1; static int z; new Point(1, 2)

scenes.say: Here is the problem. A small program has a global, a static, a local, and a Point made with new. Where does each live?

scenes.head: An office building
scenes.say: Think of an office. The rulebook in the lobby never changes: that is the text, your machine code. The notice board holds fixed values: data, and B S S for zeros. A pile of trays is the stack. A rented warehouse is the heap.

scenes.head: The memory map
scenes.say: Here is the map. Low addresses at the bottom. The code, main, sits in text, read only. The global g has a value, so it lives in data. Static z has none, so B S S, zero filled. The Point we asked for lives on the heap. Local and p live on the stack, at the top.
Your turn. Static z has no initial value. Which segment holds it? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: static int z;  Which segment holds z?

scenes.head: Ask the linker
scenes.say: B S S. A global with no initial value is zero filled at startup. The tool nm confirms it. Capital D is data, g. Lowercase b is B S S, z. And capital T is text, main.

output.cmd: g++ main.cpp -o app && nm -C app | grep -wE "g|z|main" | cut -c18-
output.text:
D g
T main
b z

scenes.head: Two groups of memory
scenes.say: Two groups. Lifetime: stack and heap come and go, static areas last the whole run. Size: static areas are fixed at load. Freed by: the compiler, you, or the loader. Growth: stack down, heap up, static areas never.

scenes.title: Who hands out heap memory?
scenes.statement: You write new int(42). Follow that request down to the operating system.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. You write new int of forty two. Who actually hands you the memory? We follow the request down.

scenes.head: A hotel front desk
scenes.say: Think of a hotel. You ask the front desk for a room. That desk is operator new, and on most systems it calls malloc. The allocator keeps a list of free rooms and hands one out. Only when the hotel is full does it ask the operating system for a new floor.

items.label: allocator
items.cue: keeps a list of free rooms

scenes.head: Three kinds of storage
scenes.say: A global like counter has static storage: it lasts the whole run. Inside f, the local x lives on the stack. But new int of forty two asks the heap, and p holds the address. Delete hands the memory back. When f returns, x and p vanish.

scenes.head: Let an owner allocate
scenes.say: In modern C plus plus you rarely write new. Small data goes on the stack. For heap data, let an owner hold it: a vector, or make unique. The owner frees it for you. Raw new needs exactly one delete on every path, and that is where leaks begin.
Your turn. Look at the vector of one million ints. Where do those ints live? Pause and predict.

scenes.head: A small owner, a big block
scenes.say: Heap. The vector object itself is small, a few pointers, on the stack. The million ints live in a heap block it owns. When big goes out of scope, its destructor frees that block.

chapters.title: malloc gives bytes, new gives objects

scenes.title: A Point that sets itself up
scenes.statement: Point's constructor sets x and y and prints built. Get a Point from the heap two ways: malloc and new.
scenes.say: Here is the problem. Point has a constructor that sets x and y. We get memory two ways: malloc, and new. Which one gives us a real Point?

scenes.head: Renting an office
scenes.say: Think of renting an office. Malloc hands you the keys to an empty room: raw bytes. The constructor is the furniture company. New does both, so you get a usable object.

scenes.head: Bytes versus an object
scenes.say: Malloc gives raw bytes. Nothing ran, so the Point inside is garbage, and using it is undefined behavior. New gives the same bytes, then the constructor runs inside them. Now x is one and y is two.

scenes.head: Which one built?
scenes.say: In code, the constructor prints built. Malloc for a Point runs nothing. New runs it once. So built prints one time, and the Point holds one and two.
Your turn. Both run out of memory. What does each one do? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: Out of memory: what do malloc and new do, in that order?

scenes.head: malloc versus new
scenes.say: Failure first: malloc returns NULL, new throws bad alloc. Constructor: only new runs one. Size: bytes by hand, versus computed from the type. Returns: void star, versus a typed pointer. Release: free, versus delete. Resize: realloc, versus allocate and move.

chapters.title: What new and delete really do

scenes.title: What does delete do that free doesn't?
scenes.statement: A Doc owns a string with a 100-character buffer. Release the Doc without leaking that buffer.

example.input: new Doc{...}; free(d) vs delete d

scenes.say: Here is the problem. A Doc object owns a string, and the string owns its own heap buffer. We must release the Doc without leaking that buffer.

scenes.head: Renting a flat
scenes.say: Think of renting a flat. The landlord hands over an empty flat: that is operator new. You move in: the constructor. When you leave, you move out first and clean up: the destructor. Then the landlord takes the keys back: operator delete.

scenes.head: new Widget(3), step by step
scenes.say: Step one: operator new returns raw memory, size of Widget bytes. Step two: the constructor runs inside it, and v becomes three. The pointer w comes back, already typed. Now delete w. First the destructor runs, then operator delete frees the block.

scenes.head: The same steps, by hand
scenes.say: You can split the steps yourself. Operator new only allocates. Placement new only constructs, inside memory you already have. Then the destructor is called by hand, and operator delete only frees. Vector uses this split to reserve capacity without building objects.
Your turn. A Doc made with new owns a string. You call free on it. What is the verdict? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `Doc* d = new Doc{...}; free(d);` What is the verdict?

scenes.head: free versus delete
scenes.say: Destructor: free never calls it, delete calls it first. Memory from: each only takes its own kind, and mixing is undefined behavior. Null: both do nothing, so skip the if. Custom: only delete can be overloaded.

scenes.head: When something throws
scenes.say: Two failure paths. No memory: operator new throws bad alloc. Constructor throws: new calls the matching operator delete for you, so nothing leaks. See alloc, free, caught. Classes can overload both, how memory pools hook in.

scenes.title: Free three objects from one pointer
scenes.statement: new T[3] builds three objects, but the pointer only points at the first. How does delete[] know there are three?

example.input: T* arr = new T[3]; delete[] arr;

scenes.say: Here is the problem. We build three T objects. The pointer only points at the first. So how does delete with brackets know it is three?

scenes.head: A coat check
scenes.say: Think of a coat check. Your ticket points at the first coat. The clerk wrote the count, three, on a tag just before it. Delete with brackets reads that tag, then runs three destructors.

scenes.head: Where the count hides
scenes.say: On G C C and Clang, for a type with a destructor, new stores the count in a hidden slot before the objects. The pointer arr points past it, at the first T. Delete with brackets reads the count, three. Then it runs three destructors, last to first, and frees the whole block.

scenes.head: Three destructors, one call
scenes.say: In code, new T with brackets builds three objects. Delete with brackets runs the destructor for each. Run it, and the message prints three times.
Your turn. Now write plain delete arr, without brackets, on that same array. What does the standard say? Pause and predict.
scenes.q: `T* arr = new T[3]; delete arr;` What does the standard say?

scenes.head: Mismatch: undefined
scenes.say: Undefined behavior. In practice it often runs one destructor, then hands the allocator the wrong address, so it crashes or corrupts the heap. The reverse mismatch is undefined too, even for int. The fix: a vector, and no delete at all.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: How does allocation work? Three storages: static, stack, heap. What does new call? Operator new, then the allocator, then the operating system when full. Modern advice? Stack first, owners over raw new.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Text? Read only machine code. Data and B S S? Globals and statics, with values or zero filled. Heap? Dynamic memory, alive until freed. Stack? Locals, freed at scope end, and small.
rows: locals: freed at scope end, small

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Malloc versus new? New also runs the constructor. Free versus delete? Delete runs the destructor first. Mixing them? Undefined behavior, so pair them up. On failure? Malloc returns NULL, new throws bad alloc.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: What does new do? It calls operator new for raw memory, then runs the constructor. If the constructor throws? New frees the memory for you. And delete? The reverse: destructor, then operator delete.

scenes.head: Say it in 20 seconds
scenes.say: Why delete brackets? New brackets hides a count, and only delete brackets reads it. Wrong form? Undefined behavior, even for int. Best fix? A vector, or a unique pointer to an array.
rows: `new[]` hides a count; only `delete[]` reads it

scenes.head: Practice before your interview
scenes.say: Solve these next. LeetCode two hundred six, reverse linked list: rewire heap nodes. LeetCode twenty one, merge two sorted lists: splice nodes, and know who owns them. Then add two numbers: allocate each new node with new.
So say this. Text, data, B S S, stack, heap: each variable has one home. New allocates, then constructs. Delete destructs, then frees. Brackets run every destructor.
lines: Text, data, bss, stack, heap: one home each.
`new[]` hides a count: pair it with `delete[]`.
